title: Scapece di Vasto
author: Marco Bellini
desc: Small fish lightly fried and then marinated in saffron-tinted vinegar for days, an Adriatic coastal specialty from Vasto designed originally to preserve the day's catch.
longDesc: Scapece is a preservation technique with roots stretching back to ancient Rome, and this Vasto version's distinctive saffron-yellow color comes from steeping the spice directly in the vinegar marinade the fried fish rests in for several days before eating.
ingredients: 1 kg (2.2 lb) small whole fish (such as anchovies or smelts), cleaned
equipment: Large glass or ceramic container for marinating
steps: Dredge the cleaned fish lightly in flour, shaking off the excess.
Heat vegetable oil and fry the fish in batches until golden and crisp, then drain on paper towels.
Warm the vinegar gently with the saffron and garlic, letting the saffron infuse and color the vinegar a deep yellow.
Let the vinegar mixture cool slightly.
Layer the fried fish in a glass or ceramic container and pour the warm vinegar mixture over, ensuring the fish is well covered.
Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 days, ideally longer, allowing the fish to fully absorb the marinade.
Serve cold or at room temperature.
chefTips: Small, whole fish work best for this preparation, as they fully absorb the vinegar marinade.
Letting the saffron properly infuse the warm vinegar is what gives scapece its distinctive golden color.
This dish genuinely needs time — the longer marinating period is what develops its characteristic tangy flavor.
commonMistakes: Rushing the marinating time, missing the full flavor development this preservation method depends on.
Using fish that are too large, which don't absorb the marinade as effectively.
Adding the fish to hot vinegar, which can cause it to break apart.
storage: Refrigerate in its marinade for up to 1 week.
reheating: Not applicable; served cold or at room temperature.
healthBenefits: Small fish are a good source of calcium, omega-3 fatty acids, and lean protein.
culturalNote: Scapece is one of the oldest known Italian food preservation techniques, tracing back to Roman times, and the Vasto version remains a specialty of Abruzzo's Adriatic coast.
